actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

supplementary_info.identification_information: Pseudechis porphyriacus is uniformly glossy black on the dorsal surfaces with red to cream ventral surfaces, where the red extends well up onto the lower flanks. The tip of the snout is brown (Wilson and Swan 2013).

documentation.range: This species is found throughout eastern Australia, from northern Queensland (where it has a disjunct distribution) to New South Wales, Victoria and southeastern South Australia (Cogger 2014).
documentation.population: This species was once common throughout its range. Subpopulations in New South Wales and Queensland are greatly reduced in areas recently invaded by toads, but elsewhere this species is common. In southeastern Queensland the population may be increasing again (Wilson and Swan 2013).
documentation.habitats: This species is a habitat generalist, and is most commonly found close to water (streams, swamps, lagoons), where it is often seen basking. It does however range far away from these areas and can also be found in suburban areas. It is a diurnal and viviparous species that reproduces in spring (mating occurring in October-November) and has a litter size between 8-40 young. During spring, males display high mobility travelling up to 1.2 km per day while seeking potentially reproductive females. The species has a wide dietary range: it feeds primarily on frogs, but also takes lizards, snakes, eels and other fish, birds and small mammals such as introduced rodents (Mirtschin and Davis 1985, Shine 1987, Shine and Lambeck 1990, Lunney et al. 2010, Cogger 2014).
documentation.threats: Once common throughout its range, subpopulations in Queensland and New South Wales appear to have declined dramatically, possibly due to attempted predation on the invasive Cane Toad (Rhinella marina), which was introduced to this area in the 1930s. This species is known to have a low tolerance to cane toad toxins and it feeds primarily on frogs, and it is estimated that Cane Toad will ultimately invade 41-53% of the snake's range (Phillips et al. 2003, Phillips et al. 2006). While the toad is long-established in much of the snake's range and declines are likely to have ceased in these areas, declines may be ongoing to some extent in recently-invaded areas. In a survey of 16 sites in New South Wales Jolly et al. (2015) found that the Red-belled Black Snake was the only snake species to respond negatively to the presence of toads, and that it was apparently absent from areas where toads were present even as long as 25 years post-invasion. There is some evidence that snakes in areas where Cane Toads have been long-established have adapted by rapidly evolving greater resistance to Cane Toad toxins and a preference for non-Cane Toad prey (Phillips and Shine 2006).
documentation.measures: In Queensland, under the Nature Conservation Act 1992, this species is considered Least Concern (EHP 2016). This species occurs within a large number of protected areas.
documentation.use_trade: There is no significant use of or trade in this species.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern on the basis that this species is generally common, adaptable and widespread, and despite mostly historical declines attributed to the invasion of the exotic cane toad this snake survives in areas where cane toads are long-established and subpopulations in some areas may be recovering.
